topic: The 3-2-1 backup rule: why one copy is never enough
scope_note: The 3-2-1 backup rule for non-technical employees who keep work files on a laptop. General personal practice only. No product names, no statistics, no RAID or backup-type detail, no extensions of the rule.

facts.statement: The 3-2-1 backup rule says to keep 3 copies of your data, on 2 different types of storage, with 1 copy offsite.
facts.reference_hint: US-CERT (CISA) 'Data Backup Options' guidance; widely repeated in vendor-neutral backup guidance

facts.statement: The 3 copies are counted as the original data plus 2 backups.
facts.reference_hint: Common reading of the rule in public guidance
facts.caveat: Sources phrase the count slightly differently, so the script should say 'the original plus two backups' and stay with that wording.

facts.statement: The rule is usually credited to the photographer Peter Krogh, who described it in his book on digital asset management for photographers.
facts.reference_hint: Peter Krogh, The DAM Book: Digital Asset Management for Photographers (2005)
facts.caveat: Attribution is common but not essential to the lesson; the script may omit it, and if used should say 'usually credited to'.

facts.statement: A single copy of a file is a single point of failure: if that one copy is lost, the data is gone.
facts.reference_hint: Basic reliability principle; CISA and NCSC backup guidance

facts.statement: Common causes of data loss include hardware failure, a lost or stolen device, accidental deletion, malware such as ransomware, and fire or flood.
facts.reference_hint: CISA 'Data Backup Options'; UK NCSC guidance on backing up your data

facts.statement: Different types of storage fail in different ways, so keeping copies on two different types of storage means one kind of fault is unlikely to remove every copy.
facts.reference_hint: Rationale given for the 'two media' part of the rule in public backup guidance
facts.caveat: This is the rule's rationale, not a guarantee: two faults at once can still happen. Say 'unlikely', not 'impossible'.

facts.statement: Copies kept on the same device, or in the same place, can be lost together by one event such as a drive failure, a theft, a fire or a flood.
facts.reference_hint: CISA 'Data Backup Options'; UK NCSC backup guidance

facts.statement: An offsite copy is stored in a different location from the original, so an event at the original location does not reach it.
Cloud storage is a common way to keep the offsite copy, because the data is held in a different location from your own devices.
facts.reference_hint: CISA 'Data Backup Options'; UK NCSC guidance on cloud backup

facts.statement: Ransomware can encrypt or damage backups that stay connected to the infected computer or network, so guidance advises keeping at least one backup offline or disconnected.
facts.reference_hint: CISA #StopRansomware Guide; UK NCSC 'Offline backups in an online world' and ransomware guidance
facts.caveat: Guidance says disconnected or offline backups reduce the risk, not that any backup is immune; avoid 'ransomware-proof'.

facts.statement: A file-sync service mirrors changes, so a deletion or an encrypted file can be copied to the synced location too; a sync alone is therefore not the same as a backup.
facts.reference_hint: General point in public backup guidance; the sheet author did not verify a specific CISA or NCSC passage
facts.caveat: Many sync services keep version history or a recycle bin, which can help recover files; the claim is only that sync by itself should not be assumed to be a backup. Not verified against one primary source.

facts.statement: Guidance advises testing that you can actually restore your files from a backup, because a backup you have never restored from may not work.
facts.reference_hint: CISA #StopRansomware Guide; UK NCSC backup guidance

not_claimed: Any statistic on how often drives fail or how many people lose data; none is claimed.
That a file saved on the laptop, or synced to a folder, is automatically a backup.
That 3-2-1 makes data loss impossible or ransomware harmless.
That cloud storage alone satisfies the whole rule: it covers the offsite copy only.
That the rule requires a specific product, vendor, or technology.
That more copies always means safer; copies that can fail together add little.
Extensions such as 3-2-1-1-0, RAID, or incremental versus full backups: out of scope, not claimed.
That the organisation already backs up laptops centrally: unknown, not claimed.

terms.definition: One thing whose loss means everything depending on it is lost.
A copy kept in a different location from the original.
A separate copy of data kept so it can be restored if the original is lost.
A service that mirrors a folder across devices or the cloud; changes, including deletions, are copied.
